Tergiversation is the act of being deliberately slippery — either in your words or in your loyalties. It describes a particular kind of dishonesty that doesn't involve outright lying, but rather dodging, shifting, and wriggling away from a clear, honest commitment.

It has two closely related meanings, and understanding both together gives you the full picture.
Meaning 1 — Evasion in Speech or Argument

This is when someone avoids giving a straight, honest answer by being deliberately vague, unclear, or confusing. They talk around a subject, use slippery language, and never quite commit to a definite position — all on purpose, to avoid accountability or scrutiny.

Think of a politician asked a direct question in an interview. Instead of answering it, they pivot to a different topic, speak in vague generalities, and by the end of their long-winded response, have said absolutely nothing of substance. That is tergiversation.

It's not the same as simply being confused or inarticulate. The key is deliberateness — the person knows what they're doing. They are purposefully making their position hard to pin down.

Examples:

  • The CEO's press statement was full of tergiversation — lots of corporate language, but zero actual answers about what went wrong.
  • The lawyer's tergiversation during cross-examination frustrated the judge, who demanded a direct response.
Meaning 2 — Abandoning a Cause or Belief

This is when someone deserts or betrays a position, cause, party, religion, or set of principles they previously held and publicly supported — especially in a way that seems cowardly or opportunistic.

Imagine a politician who spent years loudly championing a certain policy. Then, the moment it becomes politically inconvenient, they quietly drop it, or worse, start arguing the opposite. They haven't changed their mind through honest reasoning — they've simply flipped to wherever the wind is blowing. That flip-flopping, that betrayal of a prior stance for self-serving reasons, is tergiversation.

This meaning carries a strong sense of moral judgment. It implies not just change, but shameful or spineless change.

Examples:

  • His tergiversation on the issue of climate policy — after years of passionate advocacy — disappointed his supporters deeply.
  • The historian noted the general's tergiversation: he had switched sides not out of principle, but out of fear of losing.

At first, these two meanings might seem unrelated — one is about talking, the other is about loyalty. But they share a single soul: a lack of honest, clear, steadfast commitment.

In both cases, the person refuses to stand firm. In Meaning 1, they won't stand firm in their words. In Meaning 2, they won't stand firm in their beliefs or allegiances. Both are forms of moral and intellectual cowardice, dressed up in clever maneuvering.

You could think of it this way:

  • Meaning 1 = evasion (wriggling out of saying something clearly)
  • Meaning 2 = desertion (wriggling out of a position you once held)
The Tone and Register of This Word

Tergiversation is a formal, literary word. You won't hear it in casual conversation. It appears in academic writing, serious journalism, legal contexts, historical writing, and formal criticism. When someone uses this word, they are deliberately choosing it over simpler alternatives — and part of why they choose it is for its sharpness. It has a slightly contemptuous edge to it. Calling someone's behavior "tergiversation" is more damning than calling it "evasion" or "a change of heart."

Understanding what makes tergiversation different from similar words sharpens your understanding of it:

  • Equivocation — similar to Meaning 1, but focuses specifically on using ambiguous language that could mean two different things at once. Tergiversation is broader and implies more deliberate slipperiness.
  • Prevarication — means speaking in a misleading or evasive way; very close to Meaning 1 of tergiversation, but tergiversation can also cover the betrayal of a position (Meaning 2), which prevarication cannot.
  • Apostasy — similar to Meaning 2, but apostasy specifically refers to abandoning a religion or faith. Tergiversation applies to any cause, belief, or position.
  • Flip-flopping — a casual, informal version of Meaning 2. Tergiversation is the formal, weighted equivalent.
  • Vacillation — means going back and forth indecisively. Tergiversation implies more cunning and self-interest than simple indecision.

If you want a mental anchor for this word, think of a slippery eel. An eel that won't stay in your hand — it twists, it turns, it slides away. Tergiversation is intellectual and moral behavior that does exactly that: it slides away from clear truth, clear commitment, or clear loyalty, right when you need it most.

Tergiversation is the noun for two acts united by cowardice and dishonesty:

  1. Deliberately evading a straight answer through vague, shifty language.
  2. Abandoning a cause, belief, or position — especially for self-serving or cowardly reasons.

It is always intentional, always somewhat contemptible in the judgment it carries, and always about someone who refuses to commit to honesty, clarity, or principle.
